title: The Samaritans
lead: A people of the central hill country who worship the God of Israel at Mount Gerizim and keep their own form of the five books of Moses, the Samaritan Pentateuch. Jews and Samaritans quarreled for centuries over where God should be worshiped (John 4:20); a small Samaritan community still lives at Mount Gerizim and in Holon, Israel.

sections.b: Second Kings says that after Assyria took the northern kingdom (722 BC), it settled foreign peoples in Samaria, who worshiped the LORD alongside their own gods (2 Kings 17:24–41). Jewish tradition took this as the Samaritans' origin and called them Cuthites. The Samaritans tell it differently: they are the descendants of the northern tribes, especially Ephraim and Manasseh, who stayed in the land and kept the true place of worship at Gerizim, while the Jews followed a later, mistaken shrine at Jerusalem. Most historians think the full split came slowly, between the Persian period and the destruction of the Gerizim temple by John Hyrcanus about 110 BC.

sections.h: Samaritans in the Bible after the exile
sections.b: When the exiles returned, the people of the land offered to help rebuild the temple, were refused, and then opposed the work (Ezra 4:1–5). Sanballat, the governor of Samaria, mocked and threatened Nehemiah's wall-building (Nehemiah 4:1–8), and a grandson of the high priest married his daughter and was driven out (Nehemiah 13:28). These figures are not called Samaritans in the text, but later readers saw the start of the quarrel in them.

By Jesus' time Jews and Samaritans avoided each other (John 4:9). Jesus talks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, near Gerizim, about where God should be worshiped (John 4:4–42). He makes a Samaritan the hero of a parable about loving one's neighbor (Luke 10:30–37), and of ten men healed of skin disease only a Samaritan comes back to give thanks (Luke 17:11–19). After Jesus' death, Philip preaches in Samaria and many believe (Acts 8:4–25), as Jesus had said (Acts 1:8).
